# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is the strongest document in the series, and it answers most of the open questions directly. It adds log-based hours to address unclaimed work, registers the mediation test before the outcomes were available, reports an awkward finding about the control offices instead of burying it, and puts a correctly bounded caveat on the Halden subset ("an upper bound… not an estimate for organisations in general").

It also confirms the point I suspected about the meta-analysis. All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, so the "no sign of decay" claim was resting on the most inflated designs.

The arithmetic checks out:
- 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5% (logs)
- 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8% (timesheets)
- 34.9 / 40.3 → −13.4%
- 96.8 / 86.6 → +11.8%
- Mediation shares sum to 100%

I found six issues. The first two matter most, because they bear on the decay estimate itself.

## 1. The summary mixes a change of measure with decay

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." But 12.5% is a **timesheet** figure and 8.5% is a **log** figure. The like-for-like comparison, which the body text uses correctly, is **12.5% → 9.8%**:
- About 2.7 points of the drop is the change over time.
- About 1.3 points comes from switching to the stricter hours measure.

The summary should give the timesheet comparison for the trend and present 8.5% as the best current level estimate.

Relatedly, §5's "declined by about a quarter" is stated as a fact, but no interval is reported for the decline itself. The two estimates' intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 and +4.6 to +15.2). The authors criticise the meta-analysis for treating "no detected decay" as "no decay." The same discipline applies here. Report the change with its CI from the panel model, and say "consistent with modest fading."

## 2. Control contamination partly explains the decline

The month-15 meeting audit in two control offices is reported as an aside, but it directly affects the main estimate:
- Two of the seven control offices raised output per hour by about 4.1% from month 15 onward.
- That lifts the control-arm mean by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ **1.2 points**, which shrinks the treated-vs-control difference.
- The like-for-like decline being explained is only about 2.7 points.

So a substantial share of the apparent "fading" could be the control group partly taking up the treatment's active ingredient. The paper should:
- report the 24-month estimates with those two offices excluded, or with an indicator for post-audit months, as a sensitivity analysis;
- discuss contamination in the main results, not only in the "unplanned observation" section;
- note that this biases the per-hour estimate **toward zero**, which strengthens the case against the "entirely an artifact" claim.

## 3. Mediation: "confirms" is too strong, and the effective sample is 14

- **Wording.** The summary says the mediation test "confirms" the meetings mechanism. Mediation estimates rest on sequential ignorability, which the limitations section rightly says a cluster trial can't guarantee. Use "supports" or "is consistent with."
- **Clustering.** The paper credits "a larger sample of office-months," but office-months within an office aren't independent. The effective sample for the meetings–output relationship is about 14 offices. A CI of 28–66% for a mediated share is fairly narrow for 14 clusters. Say how clustering was handled. If the CI came from a bootstrap, was it resampled by office?
- **Independence of the confirmatory test.** It was registered at month 11, after the exploratory finding, using the same seven treated offices that generated the hypothesis. If the office-months include months 1–9, part of the confirmatory data overlaps the exploratory data. Repeating the analysis on months 12–24 only would make it a cleaner out-of-sample test.
- **An accounting cross-check.** If meeting time produced nothing, cutting it would raise output per hour mechanically. Using the reported figures:
  - Non-meeting hours fell by about 3.6% (hours −11%, meetings −3.3 h difference-in-differences).
  - That implies a per-hour gain of roughly 0.964 / 0.89 − 1 ≈ **8%**, close to the whole observed 8.5%.

  The 47% mediation estimate is lower, which presumably means meetings had some value or that calendar time overstates real meeting time. The two approaches bracket the meetings share at roughly half to nearly all of the gain. That's worth stating, because it bears directly on the "reorganise without cutting hours" question raised in the unplanned observation.

## 4. The reversion summary stretches one case

The summary says all three Halden reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." Two did: a hospitality group and a retail chain. The third, a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**, is discretionary work under the meta-analysis's own coding scheme. Deadline pressure isn't coverage. That reversion is evidence that discretionary work can also fail under reduced hours, and folding it into the coverage story hides that.

## 5. Cost is reported where it justifies stopping, but not where it would test continuing

For the counter arm, the paper reports that restoring service would raise cost per contact by about 9%. For case-processing, which remains on the reduced schedule, it gives no cost figures. Staff there receive full pay for 30 hours, may be claiming overtime, and produce about 3.4% less output per FTE. Labour cost per case closed is what the county needs in order to decide whether to continue, and it should be reported. Backlog and statutory-deadline compliance, flagged as a risk at nine months, are also still missing.

## 6. The Halden attrition misreport is still unaddressed

R. Okafor, a Halden working-paper author, is a co-author here. The Varga–Holm comment documented that seven of the nine "preparation-phase" withdrawals happened after the schedule began, mostly citing workload. This report rebuts the re-analysis's conclusion, rightly, but says nothing about its most concrete factual finding. With a Halden author on the paper, a brief acknowledgement or correction would strengthen its credibility. A competing-interests statement would also help.

## Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%).** It's still unclear whether the 30-hour schedule meant fewer days or shorter days. If fewer days, report the figure per scheduled day.
- **Resignations.** Still no counts or intervals.
- **Halden follow-up response rate.** 14 of 23 agreed, and the non-responders may include more reverters. The upper-bound framing covers this, but the response rate deserves a line in the limitations.
- **"Two-year horizon" as the re-analysis's standard.** Varga and Holm asked for at least 18 months, so 24 meets it. Still, one employer with seven offices per arm is a single study. It refutes "entirely an artifact" as a general claim; it doesn't establish the size of the effect elsewhere.

## Where the series lands

After five documents, the evidence supports roughly this:

> *In discretionary work, cutting scheduled hours by 20% reduces actual hours by 11–14%. Output per actual hour rises by about 8–12%, possibly fading modestly over two years (the decline is uncertain and partly confounded by control contamination). Output per employee ends slightly below where it started. A large share of the gain, perhaps half or more, appears to come from removing low-value meeting time, and part of that may be achievable without cutting hours. In coverage-bound work, reduced hours lower output and service unless staffing rises, at a cost of roughly 9% per unit. Claims of 20%+ gains, sector-general applicability, zero effect, and no decay have each been tested and narrowed.*

Each paper corrected the one before and then slightly overreached in the opposite direction. This report overreaches least. Its two slips are confined to the summary ("fell to 8.5%" and "confirms"), and both are easy to fix. The most useful next study is the one this paper identifies: an arm that cuts meetings **without** cutting hours. That is the only design that can separate how much of the gain comes from shorter hours and how much from reorganising the work.
